title: pandas for an analyst
description: Not "Python in general," but the slice of it used to work with data. Every technique is placed next to its SQL equivalent, and what SQL doesn't have at all (the index, copies, column types) is worked through separately.

intro.what:
pandas is a library for Python, not a separate language: what would have been a query's output in SQL becomes an object in memory here (a DataFrame); you can filter it further, join it to another object, compute anything on it, without going back to the database.

The main technical difference from SQL is who picks the order of computation. In SQL you describe the result you want, and the engine decides how to get it. In pandas the order is yours: steps run exactly in the order you wrote them, and after every line you need to know what's now in the variable. That shapes the kind of mistakes you make, fewer silent ones than in SQL, but more of them overall, because almost any step can hand back the wrong type, the wrong shape, or a copy instead of the original data.

This track isn't "Python from scratch": it is written for people who have already been through SQL, and it explains a fair number of techniques by comparing the two. That is not a hard requirement: the tasks are solvable without SQL, the comparisons just won't add anything. Wherever a technique matches its SQL counterpart, that's said outright; wherever pandas has something SQL doesn't have at all (the index, the difference between a copy and a view, column types), it gets its own separate, detailed treatment, because that's exactly where the time goes.
intro.where:
Computing something a single query handles awkwardly: a rolling average with a window that changes by condition, or a chain of ten transformations that isn't worth cramming into one SELECT. Bringing together data from two sources that don't live in the same database, a file from an ERP and an export from an ad platform. Quickly checking a hypothesis in a notebook before turning it into a standing query or a dashboard.

Analyst job postings ask for Python constantly, and what they almost always mean is pandas specifically, not the language at large: nobody asks an analyst to write classes and services, but everybody asks them to take an export apart.
intro.idea:
An operation applies to the whole column at once, not row by row; that's vectorisation, and pandas's entire performance story is built around it. A loop over rows works, but on even medium-sized data it's slower by orders of magnitude, and that's not a style preference; it's the difference between a second and several minutes.

The second thing worth accepting right away: a DataFrame has an index, a structure separate from the data itself that decides which rows get matched to which when two objects are combined. After a groupby, the column you grouped by doesn't disappear; it moves into the index, and that's the first thing that trips up anyone arriving from SQL, where no such concept exists at all.
intro.limits:
pandas keeps the entire dataset in the process's memory, on an export of hundreds of millions of rows that hits the machine's limits far sooner than a real database would. It's a tool for exploration and one-off calculation, not for a standing report people check every day: a calculation that has to recompute itself under any slice gets written as a measure in a data model; there's a separate track for that.

And it doesn't replace SQL, it complements it: if the data already lives in a database and the aggregation fits in one query, pulling it into pandas for the same result is an extra step with an extra point of failure.
intro.bridge:
The same working question as in SQL: brand «Nettora»'s revenue falling by almost half. Here you'll assemble it through groupby and merge (with the same meaning as INNER JOIN and GROUP BY), but the result doesn't vanish after one query; it stays an object you can keep turning: build a chart from it, run it through another filter, save it as an intermediate step.

In the data model, that same number becomes a measure that isn't computed once but recalculates itself under any slice, and that's the next step once the pandas version already makes sense to you step by step.

skills.title: DataFrame and Series
skills.summary: I read data into a DataFrame and distinguish a table from a single column, a Series, which has its own set of methods.

skills.title: The index: a DataFrame's third dimension
skills.summary: I remember that a DataFrame has an index, and I'm not surprised when a column "disappears" after groupby; it moved into the index.

skills.title: Selecting and filtering
skills.summary: I select rows with a boolean mask and columns through loc, without confusing lookup by label with lookup by position.

skills.title: Column types
skills.summary: I check dtypes before computing anything, and I understand why "summing numbers" glued strings together, and why whole numbers turned fractional on their own.

skills.title: groupby and agg
skills.summary: I build a summary with groupby, and I know ahead of time what comes back (a Series or a DataFrame) and what ends up in the index.

skills.title: transform vs. agg and apply
skills.summary: I return a value at the source granularity through transform instead of computing a summary and gluing it back on, the pandas version of a window function.

skills.title: NaN and gaps
skills.summary: I remember that NaN isn't equal to itself, and that groupby silently drops rows with a missing key by default.

skills.title: merge and row multiplication
skills.summary: I join tables knowing the key's cardinality, and I check it with validate, not after the total has doubled.

skills.title: Exploring the data
skills.summary: I look at the data before computing anything: value_counts by slice, describe by measure, and I catch an outlier or a stray category before it reaches a report.

skills.title: pivot, pivot_table and melt
skills.summary: I move a table between wide and long format and pick whichever one the next step of the calculation needs.

skills.title: Tidy data
skills.summary: I bring data to "one row, one observation; one column, one variable" and understand that this saves steps rather than just tidying up the code.

skills.title: Dates and time series
skills.summary: I cast a column to datetime, change a series' frequency with resample, and compute rolling windows with rolling.

skills.title: Chains, views and copies
skills.summary: I write transformations as a chain through assign and don't run into SettingWithCopyWarning, because I understand where a copy arises and where a view onto the source data does.

skills.title: Vectorization
skills.summary: I replace row loops and apply with a vectorized operation, and I understand that the difference here isn't style, it's an order of magnitude.

tasks.title: Price list for a promo
tasks.brief: The summer catalog only takes drinks from the «Aqualis» and «Fruvia» brands, and only items priced above 100 ¥; cheap ones don't go into a promo.
tasks.goal: Return sku_code, product_name, brand, list_price for products of these two brands priced strictly above 100.
hints: A list of values for one column is conveniently checked with .isin([...]), the pandas equivalent of SQL IN.
"Strictly above" is >, not >=. Conditions are combined with & (ampersand), not and — and doesn't work on a pandas column.
tasks.explain: & and | are not and/or: and/or in Python expect a single boolean value, while a column is a Series of thousands of True/False at once, and and has no way to decide what to do with it. & and | compute logic element-wise, and that's the only option that works for a pandas filter. Hence the parentheses around each condition: & binds tighter than ==, so without parentheses Python would first evaluate 'Aqualis' & (list_price > 100) and fail with a TypeError about "rand_", a message that gives no hint at the cause unless you remember operator precedence.

tasks.title: and instead of &
tasks.brief: A colleague wrote a filter out of an old Python habit (with and) and got not a result but an error, right in front of the client.
tasks.goal: Determine what happens when the code runs.
tasks.predictQuestion: What happens when this code runs, if dim_product has more than one row?

options.label: Returns products of the «Aqualis» brand priced above 100 ¥
options.why: That's what would happen with & instead of and. and tries to reduce each condition to a single True/False before the comparison even happens, and that's exactly the step where everything fails.

options.label: Fails with an error: 'The truth value of a Series is ambiguous'
options.why: and requires a single boolean value on each side, and (dim_product['list_price'] > 100) is a Series of thousands of True/False values. pandas can't decide what to treat as "true" here, and honestly fails with a ValueError instead of guessing.

options.label: Returns an empty DataFrame: no row matched
options.why: That would be a quiet, much more harmless outcome. In reality pandas doesn't stay silent: it can't evaluate and over an entire column and raises a ValueError before it ever gets to selecting rows.

options.label: Returns every row of the original table, unfiltered
options.why: If and were simply ignored, that would be plausible. But and is part of the Python language, not pandas, and it tries to evaluate both operands as bool at once, which is impossible for a Series.

hints: and is a Python-language operator, not a pandas one. It expects one True/False on each side.
(dim_product['list_price'] > 100) isn't a single value, it's a column of True/False, one per row.
tasks.explain: The message 'The truth value of a Series is ambiguous' is the most common beginner's mistake in pandas, and it's worth seeing consciously once, rather than in a panic in the middle of a real task. The rule is simple: between two conditions on columns it's always & or |, and and/or are only for two already-resolved single values (two numbers, say).

tasks.title: E-com customers for the logistics report
tasks.brief: Logistics puts together a separate report for marketplace warehouses (they're serviced differently from retail) and needs a short list of these outlets.
tasks.goal: Return customer_id, customer_name and city only for customers with channel = 'ecom'.
hints: The channel value is a string, compared with ==, like an ordinary text value.
The second blank is one more column name in the list passed to .loc.
tasks.explain: loc[mask, column_list] isn't two different techniques, it's one call with two parts: to the left of the comma you decide which rows to take, to the right which columns to keep. In SQL that's WHERE and the SELECT list; here it's one operation, because both are just indexing into the table.

tasks.title: The «Forte» line for the category report
tasks.brief: The category manager is pulling the strengthened «Forte» line into a separate section of the quarterly report; there aren't many of these products, and looking them up one by one in the reference table by hand isn't an option.
tasks.goal: Return sku_code, product_name for products whose product_name contains the substring 'Forte'.
hints: Text methods on a string column are called through .str, the pandas equivalent of LIKE '%...%'.
.str.contains('Forte') returns a boolean column, which you can plug straight into .loc as a mask.
tasks.explain: .str isn't decoration, it's a necessity: without it Python would try to call .contains() on the whole column at once and fail, because a Series as a whole has no such method. .str opens access to string methods element by element, for each value of the column separately, the pandas equivalent of how SQL applies LIKE to every row of a table.

tasks.title: A view for the buyer
tasks.brief: A buyer asks for a short view of products for price reconciliation: just the code, name and price (no service fields like launch_date).
tasks.goal: Return sku_code, product_name, list_price for all products.
hints: A list of columns is passed as a list inside square brackets: df[['a', 'b']].
No row filtering is needed here, just select columns, all products stay.
tasks.explain: dim_product[['sku_code', 'product_name', 'list_price']] is df[column_list], and the result is always a DataFrame, even if the list has one column. The outer brackets address the table, the inner ones are the list of names itself. It's easy to confuse this with df['sku_code'] (one column, no nested brackets); that gives a Series, not a table, see the next task.

tasks.title: One bracket or two
tasks.brief: A colleague copied code from an old report, and instead of a table with one column got something that won't accept .rename(columns=...).
tasks.goal: Understand the difference between dim_product['brand'] and dim_product[['brand']].
tasks.predictQuestion: What's the fundamental difference between a and b?

options.label: a is a Series (a one-dimensional column), b is a DataFrame with one column, "brand"
options.why: Single square brackets with a column name return a Series, the column itself. Double brackets are df[list], and even a list of one name gives a DataFrame, a two-dimensional table.

options.label: The result is the same: these are two equivalent ways of writing the same thing
options.why: The values match, but the types differ: a is a Series, b is a DataFrame. The difference surfaces on the very first call meant for a table: a Series has neither .columns nor .merge(), and while .rename(columns=...) does exist, it doesn't accept the columns parameter there and fails with a TypeError; there's nothing to rename in a Series, it has one name of its own instead of a list of columns.

options.label: a will raise an error: that's not how columns are selected
options.why: df['col'] is the standard, most common way to get a single column as a Series. There's no error here.

options.label: a is a DataFrame with one column, b is a Series
options.why: It's exactly the reverse: one level of brackets is a Series, two levels (a list inside the brackets) is a DataFrame.

hints: The number of levels of square brackets is the answer itself: one level versus a list inside.
A DataFrame has columns and their names; a Series has only values and one name of its own.
tasks.explain: This is the most common cause of "AttributeError: 'Series' object has no attribute ..." for people just starting out: a method that exists on DataFrame gets called on a Series, because there ended up being one fewer pair of brackets than expected. The habit worth building: after selecting columns, check the type of the result, not just the values.

tasks.title: Regions for a demographic summary
tasks.brief: A demographics report needs a short slice of regions: just the name and population, no macro-region or tier.
tasks.goal: Return region_name and population for all regions.
hints: Both blanks are column names, each in quotes, separated by a comma.
The outer brackets are already there; they mean "a list of columns from the table".
tasks.explain: The same df[[...]] technique works for any table: on the outside, addressing the DataFrame by a list of columns, on the inside, the list of name strings itself. The order in the list is the order of the columns in the result, just like a SELECT list in SQL.

tasks.title: Manager 1.0
tasks.brief: An HR analyst opens the employee extract and can't understand why the manager's code is 1.0, not 1: "Is this a fractional employee?"
tasks.goal: Understand why manager_id prints with a decimal point.
tasks.predictQuestion: Five managers have an empty manager_id (they have no boss of their own). Why does that make the ENTIRE manager_id column display as 1.0, 2.0, ... rather than 1, 2, ...?

options.label: The column has gaps, and the plain integer type int64 can't hold NaN: pandas upgrades the whole column to float64
options.why: NaN is a special floating-point value, and int64 physically cannot hold it. As soon as an integer column has even one gap, pandas converts the entire column to float64, hence the decimal point on every value, even the ones that are present.

options.label: It's a bug in the dataset: someone forgot to store manager_id as an integer
options.why: The data are fine: pandas chooses the type itself when reading, and with gaps present int64 simply isn't physically available for that column; this is library behavior, not a flaw in the source.

options.label: pandas always stores numeric ids as float64: that's a general rule for every column
options.why: Not general: rep_id in the same table is also numbers, but it has no gaps, and that column stayed int64, without a single decimal point. The cause is specifically NaN, not the fact that the values are identifiers.

options.label: This only happens in old pandas versions: in newer ones the ids will stay whole
options.why: This is a fundamental limitation of the NumPy int64 type (it simply has no representation for "no value"), not a version bug. There's a separate nullable type, Int64 with a capital letter, that can hold both integers and gaps, but that isn't the default behavior.

hints: The five managers have role = 'manager', and none of them has their own manager_id, meaning the column contains NaN.
int64 is a type with no NaN. Since a gap needs to fit somewhere, pandas picks the nearest type that can hold it.
tasks.explain: One and the same cause sits behind two frequent confusions: "why is the id fractional" and "why did the sum of numbers turn into NaN when just one row was missing." pandas types a column as a whole, not value by value, and a single gap in an integer column changes the type of every one of its values at once.

tasks.title: Who in the company has no manager
tasks.brief: The org chart needs a list of top-level employees, the ones who have no manager of their own.
tasks.goal: Return rep_id, rep_name, team for employees whose manager_id is empty.
hints: "Empty" in pandas is NaN, and checking for it is a separate method: .isna(), not == None and not == NaN.
The result of .isna() is already a boolean mask, and it can be plugged straight into .loc.
tasks.explain: NaN is the only value in Python that isn't equal to itself, so df['x'] == None or df['x'] == float('nan') don't find gaps at all. .isna() is the only reliable way to check for them, and it's the same gap that turned manager_id into float64 in the previous task, two problems, one cause.

tasks.title: Bringing the id back to whole numbers
tasks.brief: A colleague asks for an extract for the HR system, where manager_id has to arrive without a decimal point; the import doesn't accept "6.0" as an employee code.
tasks.goal: Return rep_id, rep_name, manager_id, casting manager_id to an integer type that still allows gaps.
hints: Plain int64 won't work here; the column has gaps, and int64 can't hold them.
pandas has a separate nullable type, capitalized at the start of its name; it holds both whole numbers and gaps.
tasks.explain: Int64 (capitalized) isn't a typo and isn't the same as int64: it's a separate pandas nullable type that prints gaps as <NA> rather than as a floating-point NaN, and stores the rest of the values as true integers, no decimal point. Plain int64 doesn't fit this task at all: .astype('int64') on this same column fails with IntCastingNaNError ("cannot convert NA to integer"), and no rewording gets around it, because int64 physically has no room for a gap.

tasks.title: Where did product_id go
tasks.brief: An intern computed sales by product and sent a screenshot: columns units and product_id, but only units is there, and above it sits a strange caption product_id, as if it were a heading rather than a column.
tasks.goal: Understand where product_id went after the grouping.
tasks.predictQuestion: The result is a Series with one column of units values. Where did product_id end up?

options.label: It became the index of the result: labeled to the left of the values, but it isn't counted as a separate column
options.why: groupby makes the grouping column the index of the result by default. It's visible, just not in the position of an ordinary column, and code expecting product_id as df['product_id'] won't find it.

options.label: It's gone for good: you'll have to group again while keeping product_id separately
options.why: Nothing is lost: product_id is alive in the index, and .reset_index() returns it as a column again at any moment, with no need to regroup.

options.label: It stayed an ordinary column, it's just not shown in this particular output
options.why: It is shown: that thing that looks like a "caption on top" is exactly product_id: it's the index of the Series, not a missing column.

options.label: groupby deletes the grouping column from the result entirely by default
options.why: It doesn't delete it, it moves it, into the index. That's an important difference: what's in the index isn't deleted, it just has to be accessed differently from an ordinary column.

hints: groupby('col') isn't the same as removing col from the result.
Every DataFrame and Series has an index: its own label column on the left of the values, which isn't physically part of the list of ordinary columns.
tasks.explain: SQL has no such distinction; GROUP BY product_id simply leaves product_id as an ordinary column of the result. pandas has a third dimension (the index), and this is the first place where the analogy with SQL stops matching one to one.

tasks.title: Brand by product code
tasks.brief: A merchandiser is reconciling warehouse stock against the shelf and knows only the product_id from the delivery note. They need to quickly check which brand that is.
tasks.goal: Return product_id and brand for the product with product_id = 5, setting product_id as the table's index and looking up the row with .loc.
hints: set_index('product_id') makes product_id the index; after that, rows are looked up through it via .loc, not through a mask on a column.
The number in square brackets inside .loc is the index label to look up, not a position.
tasks.explain: .loc[[5], ['brand']] is a lookup by index label, not by condition: the same spirit as a primary key in SQL, only explicitly assigned via set_index rather than implied. A list of one element, [5], not bare 5, that way the result stays a table, rather than turning into a single-value Series.

tasks.title: Bringing product_id back as a column
tasks.brief: The result of the grouping needs to be merged with another table on product_id, and merge looks for it as an ordinary column, not as an index.
tasks.goal: After grouping by product_id, return product_id as an ordinary column again.
hints: You need the method that reverses what groupby does with the grouping column by default.
The method's name says it plainly: it "resets" the index back into ordinary columns.
tasks.explain: .reset_index() is the most common next step after groupby if the grouping result is going to be used further: in a merge, in a comparison with another table, when writing to a file. Without it, product_id stays in the index, and an attempt at merge(..., on='product_id') won't find such a column.

tasks.title: Assortment and price by division
tasks.brief: The category manager is comparing the price spread between FMCG and Pharma before planning next quarter's price list.
tasks.goal: Group dim_product by division and return three columns: division, n_sku (the number of products, count on sku_code) and avg_price (the average list_price, rounded to one decimal place).
hints: Named aggregation: .agg(column_name=('column', 'function')): gives flat names right away, no MultiIndex headers.
as_index=False returns division as an ordinary column right away, not as an index, no need to call reset_index() separately.
tasks.explain: In SQL this would be GROUP BY division with two aggregates in the SELECT. Here it's the same thing, one call to .agg(...) with named results: each name=('source_column', 'function') immediately becomes a separate column with the name you want. The alternative, a list of functions, .agg(['count', 'mean']), is worse for two reasons at once. Applied to the whole table it fails with a TypeError: you can't average product_name or brand, and a list of functions gives no way to say which one applies to which column. And narrowed to one column (dim_product.groupby('division')[['list_price']].agg(['count', 'mean'])), both functions land in a two-level header ('list_price', 'count'), which still has to be picked apart afterward. Named aggregation removes both problems: it names the source, the function, and the result's name all at once.

tasks.title: What order will the brands land in
tasks.brief: An intern groups products by brand and expects to see them in the order the brands first appeared in the file, and gets something else.
tasks.goal: Understand the order groupby puts groups in by default.
tasks.predictQuestion: dim_product has 47 rows, brands appear in mixed order. In what order will the first three brands land in the result?

options.label: Alphabetically: «Vitanor», «Gastrivo», «Aqualis», that is, in order of the key's values, not the order of rows in the source table
options.why: groupby sorts groups by the key's value by default (sort=True); this behavior is always on unless sort=False is passed explicitly. The row order in the source table has no effect on the result.

options.label: In the order the brands first appeared in the file
options.why: That would happen with sort=False, but that isn't the default. Without an explicit sort=False, groupby always sorts by key.

options.label: In descending average price: from the most expensive brand to the cheapest
options.why: groupby doesn't sort by the value of the measure (list_price) on its own; that would need a separate .sort_values() after the aggregation. By default it's the grouping key that gets sorted, not the result.

options.label: The order is unpredictable and can differ on every run
options.why: The result is deterministic: the same table always gives the same group order, because the sorting is by the key's value, not by randomness or memory layout.

hints: groupby has a sort parameter, and it's True by default.
It's specifically the grouping key (brand) that gets sorted, not the aggregation result (mean).
tasks.explain: In SQL, GROUP BY without a separate ORDER BY gives no guaranteed result order under any standard. pandas is exactly the opposite: sorting by key is on by default, and if you need the row order of the source table (for speed on a very large grouping, say), that's a separate, deliberate choice, sort=False.

tasks.title: Division × category matrix
tasks.brief: Before assembling the assortment matrix, someone needs a quick view of how many SKUs fall into each "division / category" pair.
tasks.goal: Group dim_product by two columns at once, division and category, and count sku_code in each pair.
hints: Grouping by several columns at once is a list of names inside groupby([...]), not two separate calls.
Both blanks are column names in quotes: division first, then category.
tasks.explain: groupby([...]) with a list is a direct equivalent of GROUP BY division, category in SQL: every unique combination of values from the two columns becomes its own group. as_index=False matters here just as much as in single-key grouping; without it both columns would go into a MultiIndex instead of staying ordinary columns of the result.

tasks.title: How concentrated a distributor's purchases are
tasks.brief: The distributor KAM is preparing annual-terms negotiations and wants to understand concentration: whose purchases are spread across the whole assortment, and whose few positions make up the lion's share of volume; the discount conversation goes differently with the latter.
tasks.goal: Add a line_share column to fact_sellin: this row's share of net_amount in the sum of net_amount for the same distributor_id over the whole period of the table.
hints: transform, unlike agg, returns a result the same length as the source table, good for gluing a summary back onto every row.
.groupby('distributor_id')['net_amount'].transform('sum') is the sum of net_amount for the distributor, repeated in every row of that distributor.
tasks.explain: agg() would collapse the group into one row; 12 distributors would give 12 rows, not 15,362. transform() returns the same number of rows as the source table, plugging its group's total into every row, the distributor's whole purchase volume across the table, repeated in every one of its order lines. From there the share comes out of a single division, with no separate merge needed to "glue the summary back on", the same thing a SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY distributor_id) window function does in SQL. A check on the spot: line_share summed over the whole table has to come to exactly 12, one per distributor.

tasks.title: sum() and transform('sum'): different length
tasks.brief: A colleague plugged in sum() where a transform was needed, and got a column that's almost all NaN instead of each sale's share.
tasks.goal: Understand how the results of sum() and transform('sum') differ after the same grouping.
tasks.predictQuestion: fact_sellout has 118,449 rows and 47 unique product_id values. How many rows will a and b have?

options.label: a has 47 rows, b has 118,449: sum() collapses the group into one row, transform returns a result for every source row
options.why: sum() is an ordinary aggregation: the group collapses into a single value, and the result is a Series with one row per product_id. transform('sum') computes the same thing, but repeats it in every row of the source group, keeping the source table's length.

options.label: Both have 47 rows: both methods aggregate the data the same way
options.why: transform doesn't aggregate in that sense: it's specifically built not to change the number of rows, otherwise a share column couldn't be glued back onto the source table element by element.

options.label: Both have 118,449 rows: since it's the same measure (units), the result's length shouldn't change
options.why: sum() after groupby always collapses the group; that's its whole point as an aggregating function. The difference between sum() and transform('sum') is precisely whether the result collapses the group or not, not which function is computed inside.

options.label: a has 118,449, b has 47: the options are swapped
options.why: It's exactly the reverse: the short result (47 rows, one per product) comes from the plain aggregation sum(), the long one (118,449, one per source row) comes from transform.

hints: agg/sum is a per-group summary, transform is that same summary repeated on every row of the group.
If the result is going to sit as a new column next to the source data, the length has to match; that's the first sign you need transform specifically.
tasks.explain: Dividing result['units'] (118,449 rows) by a (47 rows) doesn't give what was intended: pandas aligns the two objects by index, and their indexes differ, row numbers versus product_id. The result turns out sneakier than a solid wall of NaN: labels 1…47 will coincide, and 47 rows will get a real number computed from an unrelated pairing of "this row / that unrelated product," while the remaining 118,402 come out empty. There's no runtime error at all, just a column that looks half-plausible.

tasks.title: Each product's biggest sale
tasks.brief: A logistics analyst is looking, for each product, for its single largest delivery: a suspicion of stockpiling ahead of a promo, visible only at the level of individual sales.
tasks.goal: Add a revenue_rank column with this sale's rank by revenue within its product_id (1 = the product's largest sale), descending.
hints: .rank() is the pandas equivalent of the RANK/DENSE_RANK/ROW_NUMBER window functions: it also needs a group and an order, just through the method's parameters instead of an OVER clause.
method='min' gives RANK (tied values get the same rank, the next one jumps over the skipped places); method='dense' would give DENSE_RANK, 'first' would give ROW_NUMBER.
tasks.explain: rank() inside groupby is a direct equivalent of RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...): the partition is set by groupby, the order and direction are parameters of rank() rather than a separate ORDER BY. Choosing method changes the same thing that choosing between RANK, DENSE_RANK and ROW_NUMBER changes in SQL: they each decide differently what to do with a spot that looks "claimed twice" when values tie.

tasks.title: 132 customers instead of 144
tasks.brief: A financial controller is reconciling the "customers by rep" report against the total customer count in the reference table; the sums don't match, and it's unclear where twelve went missing.
tasks.goal: Understand where rows disappear when grouping by a column with gaps.
tasks.predictQuestion: dim_customer has 144 customers, and 12 of them (all with channel = 'distributor') have an empty rep_id. What will this sum equal?

options.label: 132: groupby drops rows with a missing key by default, before the count is even taken
options.why: dropna=True is the default behavior: the 12 customers without a rep_id don't fall into any group and aren't counted anywhere, so the sum across all groups is smaller than the total row count.

options.label: 144: groupby counts every row, including the ones where the grouping key is empty
options.why: That would be true with dropna=False. By default pandas quietly excludes rows with NaN in the grouping key from the result entirely.

options.label: 12: pandas will group only the customers with no rep, and count the other 132 as one shared gap
options.why: It's the reverse: gaps in the key don't form their own group by default, they drop out completely. The other 132 customers, meanwhile, group normally, each under its own rep_id.

options.label: The code will fail with an error: groupby doesn't accept a column with gaps as a key
options.why: There's no error: NaN in a grouping key is an ordinary situation, and pandas handles it quietly by excluding rows, not by refusing to run the grouping.

hints: groupby has a dropna parameter, and it's True by default.
"Quietly" is the key word: pandas doesn't report the excluded rows with any warning.
tasks.explain: One and the same setting sits behind two frequent confusions: "the report's sum is smaller than the total count" and "this category didn't show up in the result at all." The check is simple. Compare the sum of the grouping result to the row count of the source table: if it's smaller, some rows were excluded because of a gap in the key.

tasks.title: Customers by rep: with nothing lost
tasks.brief: The same report, but done right: the sum has to match the reference table's total customer count, including the 12 who have no rep at all.
tasks.goal: Count the number of customers per rep_id, including a separate group for customers with no rep, and return columns rep_id, n_customers.
hints: dropna=False is a groupby parameter that keeps the NaN key as its own group instead of dropping its rows.
After groupby(...)['customer_id'].count() you'll get a Series; .reset_index(name='n_customers') turns it into a table with the column name you want.
tasks.explain: dropna=False is the only difference from the "ordinary" grouping, and it changes everything: without it, the sum of n_customers over the result equals 132, not 144, and there's no way to tell from that single report where the remaining 12 customers went. NaN in rep_id in this dataset isn't a defect, it's a fact: distributors have no assigned rep, they're handled by the whole team.

tasks.title: Labeling customers with no rep
tasks.brief: The rep report goes into a BI system, where a NaN in the key looks like a load error; a readable label is needed instead of an empty value.
tasks.goal: Before grouping, replace gaps in rep_id with a clear label, -1, so the group stays put without needing dropna=False on the receiving end.
hints: fillna(-1) replaces NaN with a specific value before grouping; after that it isn't a gap anymore, it's an ordinary key, -1.
.assign(rep_id=...) returns a new table with the replaced column, without touching the original dim_customer.
tasks.explain: fillna before grouping and dropna=False after grouping solve the same problem in different ways: dropna=False keeps NaN as is (that's NaN in the final table), while fillna(-1) turns the gap into an ordinary value ahead of time, one you can work with further without special parameters, say, if the next step compares rep_id against another table where comparisons with NaN don't work.

tasks.title: 110,480 sales instead of 11,048
tasks.brief: An analyst joins fact_sellout to dim_promo by brand, to mark the promo period next to every sale, and afterward revenue is off by multiples from the report.
tasks.goal: Understand what happens when you join on a key that's non-unique on both sides.
tasks.predictQuestion: The «Nettora» brand has 11,048 rows in fact_sellout and 10 different promos in dim_promo (all with brand = 'Nettora'). How many rows will merged give for this brand?

options.label: 110,480: each of the 11,048 sales got glued to each of the brand's 10 promos
options.why: merge doesn't check key uniqueness on either side by default: if there are 11,048 rows on the left with brand = 'Nettora' and 10 on the right, every pair with a matching brand produces a separate result row, 11,048 × 10.

options.label: 11,048: one per source sale, with the promo just noted alongside
options.why: That would be the case if the join were on promo_id, dim_promo's unique key. Joining on brand doesn't distinguish the 10 promos from each other, so every sale shows up 10 times in the result, not once.

options.label: 10: merge will collapse all of the brand's sales down to one row per promo
options.why: merge never collapses rows; that's what groupby does. merge only joins rows that match on the key, and if there are multiple matches on both sides, the row count goes up, not down.

options.label: The code will fail with an error: merge doesn't allow joining on a column with repeated values
options.why: There's no error: merge, by default (without validate=), doesn't check key cardinality at all. It honestly performs the cross-match for every pair, silently, without a single warning.

hints: merge doesn't check by default that the join key is unique on at least one side.
10 promos for one brand is the same as if there were 10 promos for one product: a tenfold blow-up is expected when the key doesn't distinguish them from each other.
tasks.explain: This is the same fan-out as in SQL (see sql-fanout): an INNER JOIN on a key that's non-unique on both sides multiplies rows rather than flagging them. merge() in pandas behaves identically; the library only checks that values match, not that a one-to-one relationship was intended. The right key here is promo_id, which already exists in fact_sellout and points to a specific promo, not the brand as a whole.

tasks.title: The promo discount next to every sale
tasks.brief: The same question, but asked correctly: the commercial director wants to see the discount (discount_pct) next to every sale if it went through a promo, and an empty value if it didn't.
tasks.goal: Join fact_sellout to dim_promo on promo_id so that all rows of fact_sellout are kept (including sales outside any promo), adding only discount_pct.
hints: how='left' keeps all rows of fact_sellout, even where promo_id is empty, the pandas equivalent of LEFT JOIN.
promo_id is dim_promo's primary key (89 rows, 89 unique values), so joining on it doesn't multiply rows, unlike joining on brand.
tasks.explain: how='left' is mandatory here, not a stylistic detail: fact_sellout has rows with no promo (promo_id empty), and merge's default (how='inner') would quietly drop them from the result. Plus promo_id is unique in dim_promo, so joining on it is one-to-one and doesn't multiply rows, unlike the previous task, where the key was brand.

tasks.title: Guarding against another fan-out
tasks.brief: After the story about joining on brand, a colleague asks for a safeguard going forward: the code should fail with a clear error if someone mixes up the key again, instead of silently bloating the table.
tasks.goal: Repeat the join of fact_sellout to dim_promo on promo_id with how='left', adding a cardinality check: the key may repeat on the left, but must be unique on the right.
hints: validate is an optional merge parameter that checks join cardinality and fails with a MergeError if the expectation isn't met.
'many_to_one' means: on the left (fact_sellout) the key can repeat, on the right (dim_promo) it must be unique.
tasks.explain: validate='many_to_one' is a claim recorded right in the code: if a duplicate promo_id ever shows up in dim_promo, or someone by mistake joins on brand instead of promo_id, merge will fail with a MergeError instead of quietly returning a bloated table, as in the first task in this skill. It's cheap and catches exactly the mistake this walkthrough started with.

tasks.title: How many items each brand has
tasks.brief: Ahead of a conversation about assortment rotation, an analyst wants a quick look at how many SKUs fall under each brand in the catalogue, without grouping or counting by hand.
tasks.goal: Count the number of items for each value of brand in dim_product, sorted in descending order of count.
hints: value_counts() is a Series method, not a DataFrame one: first select one column with single brackets.
Descending order is the default behavior, nothing extra needs to be called.
tasks.explain: value_counts() is groupby(column).size(), sorted descending, in one short call. Unlike groupby, it's purpose-built for one task (counting how often values occur), and it's almost always the first step of exploration: not computing the metric right away, but seeing how the categories that will be used to slice the data are distributed in the first place. There are nine brands here, and the catalogue is spread evenly across them: from six items (Aqualis, Fruvia, Krosti, Milvara) down to four (Gastrivo, Rhinolar). The breadth of a line says nothing about its sales, though: a four-item brand can well out-earn a six-item one. value_counts counts rows in the reference table, not money, and confusing those two questions is the most common mistake at this very first step of exploration.

tasks.title: An average price of 230 ¥ that doesn't exist
tasks.brief: A category manager looks at .describe() over list_price for the whole product reference table and reports upstairs: "the average SKU price is 230 ¥." A colleague from pharma is surprised: isn't our average around 400?
tasks.goal: Understand what's behind the discrepancy, given that describe()'s own number isn't wrong.
tasks.predictQuestion: The mean in the output really is 230.3 ¥; describe() didn't lie. What's behind the mismatch the colleague noticed?

options.label: The column actually mixes two different divisions (FMCG with an average of 110.7 ¥ and Pharma with an average of 423.2 ¥); the overall average describes neither
options.why: describe() computes statistics over all 47 values at once, with no idea they belong to two dissimilar groups. 230.3 ¥ is the real average across the whole catalog, but it sits between the two real averages, at a point with no product at all.

options.label: describe() was computed wrong: with prices ranging from 38 to 812 ¥, the function should have split the column into groups itself
options.why: describe() knows nothing about categories inside a column, and it shouldn't: that's a limitation by design, not a computation error. Splitting into groups is a separate, deliberate step through groupby.

options.label: It's a rounding error: 230.3 is actually the average for FMCG only
options.why: The numbers don't match: FMCG's average is 110.7 ¥, not 230.3. 230.3 ¥ is the honest average across all 47 products at once, it just doesn't resemble either of the two real groups within the column.

options.label: describe()'s std would have flagged the problem right away, so if the colleague didn't look at it, that's on them
options.why: std really would hint at a wide spread, but describe() doesn't force anyone to interpret it correctly; a large std can be written off as natural price variation rather than two groups being mixed together. The danger is precisely that one number (mean) looks sufficient on its own.

hints: describe() knows nothing about categories inside a column; it computes statistics over all the values at once, however different they may be.
A suspiciously wide spread (a large std relative to the mean) is a signal to check whether different groups are mixed in the column.
tasks.explain: describe() is exploration, not a diagnosis: it honestly computes statistics over whatever it was given, and doesn't check whether the sample is homogeneous. Thorough exploration almost always includes a slice by the key category, not just an overall summary, describe() over the whole column and describe() by group can tell different stories, and here the second one is closer to the truth.

tasks.title: describe() for each division separately
tasks.brief: To avoid repeating the past mistake, the same manager wants to see describe() for each division separately right away, not one overall summary for the whole catalog.
tasks.goal: Get describe() on list_price separately for each value of division.
hints: describe() can be called not only on a whole column but on the result of a groupby too; then the statistics are computed separately for each group.
Group by the very field that hid the difference between FMCG and Pharma in the previous task.
tasks.explain: groupby(...).describe() is a way to run its own summary statistics over every group in one call, with no loop and no manually splitting the table into parts. Since the column for describe() is already chosen (['list_price']), the result stays an ordinary table: one row per division, eight statistic columns, you can compare them at a glance, not just as a single number, unlike in the previous task.

tasks.title: Revenue by brand, by quarter
tasks.brief: The commercial director wants to see 2025 revenue by brand, by quarter, in one table: brands as rows, quarters as columns, not a long list of thirty-six rows.
tasks.goal: Build a pivot table off the already-prepared merged/sub: brand in the rows, quarter in the columns, the sum of revenue in the values.
hints: pivot_table can aggregate and reshape in one call; aggfunc decides what to do if several rows land on the same brand/quarter intersection (here: many sales of different products and customers).
index becomes the rows, columns becomes the column headers, values ends up in the cells.
tasks.explain: Unlike .pivot(), which requires exactly one row per (brand, quarter) pair, pivot_table resolves this itself through aggregation: aggfunc='sum' sums up all of the brand's sales for the quarter, no matter how many source rows land in that cell. It's the same thing a conditional aggregation, CASE WHEN quarter = '2025Q1' THEN revenue END (see sql-case), does in SQL, just without spelling out every quarter explicitly in the code.

tasks.title: pivot() instead of pivot_table()
tasks.brief: A colleague tries reshaping the same dataset with .pivot() (a shorter name, quicker to type) and gets an error instead of a table.
tasks.goal: Understand why pivot() doesn't work on raw, not-yet-aggregated data.
tasks.predictQuestion: sub is the raw fact_sellout rows (customer × product × week), joined with brand and quarter, with no aggregation done beforehand. What happens when .pivot() is called?

options.label: It fails with ValueError "Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape": many rows land on each (brand, quarter) pair, and pivot expects exactly one
options.why: pivot() is a pure reshape with no aggregation: it has no way to decide what to do if several source rows claim the same result cell, and it honestly raises a ValueError instead of guessing.

options.label: It returns the same table as pivot_table: those are two names for the same operation
options.why: The names are similar, but the behavior differs: pivot_table takes an aggfunc and aggregates matches, while pivot expects there to be no matches at all, and fails if that isn't the case.

options.label: It returns a table, taking the last row in order for each cell and silently dropping the rest
options.why: pivot doesn't silently drop data; wherever several rows are found for one cell, it stops with an error rather than arbitrarily picking one of them.

options.label: It returns a table, summing the values in cells with matching brand and quarter: like pivot_table with aggfunc='sum'
options.why: Summing is exactly what pivot_table does, not pivot. pivot has no aggfunc parameter at all: it can't aggregate and doesn't try to.

hints: pivot() expects the index/columns combination to already be unique, the kind of result you'd get after a groupby.
pivot_table takes raw, not-yet-aggregated data and aggregates it itself via aggfunc.
tasks.explain: The difference is exactly the word "table": pivot is a pure reshape of the data, pivot_table is the same reshape plus a mandatory aggfunc for collisions. If the data has already been through a groupby and each row/column combination is guaranteed to have exactly one entry, pivot() runs without errors; on raw data, as here, it's almost always pivot_table.

tasks.title: Reshaping the report back to long format
tasks.brief: The same quarterly-by-brand report needs to go to a BI system that only accepts long format: one brand and one quarter per row, not a wide table.
tasks.goal: Reshape the wide table piv (brand, 2025Q1, 2025Q2) back to long format: columns brand, quarter, revenue.
hints: id_vars is the column that stays as is and doesn't get reshaped; everything else turns into pairs of "column name → value".
var_name and value_name name the two new columns: the one with the former column names and the one with their values.
tasks.explain: melt is the reverse of pivot_table: a wide table (one column per quarter) becomes a long one (one row per brand-quarter pair). id_vars fixes brand as is, while '2025Q1' and '2025Q2' stop being column names and become values in the new quarter column, exactly what's needed if the receiving system expects one row per observation.

tasks.title: 58 codes instead of 29 products
tasks.brief: An extract from the old system gives 58 different product codes instead of 29 real FMCG SKUs; some of the codes are duplicated in a different case: "nett005" and "NETT005" are the same product.
tasks.goal: Count how many unique product codes will remain in staging_raw_sellout if sku_code is cast to a single case.
hints: .str.upper() upper-cases every string in the column in one call.
nunique() counts the number of unique values, exactly what's needed to see how many codes remain after normalization.
tasks.explain: 58 → 29: exactly half of the codes were the same product, written in a different case. Casting to a single case before counting isn't cosmetic: nunique() compares strings character by character, and to it «nett005» is not the same product as «NETT005». SQL has the same idea (COUNT(DISTINCT UPPER(sku_code))), but SQLite's UPPER and LOWER are limited to the ASCII range (see sql-027), while pandas's .str.upper() follows full Unicode rules. You can't see the difference on these codes, because they're Latin; it shows up on the first reference table with diacritics or Cyrillic, and it shows up silently, as under-merging, not as an error. Hence the working habit: test case normalization on data whose alphabet isn't only English.

tasks.title: Case and spaces aren't normalization yet
tasks.brief: After the product codes, a colleague moves on to customer names and applies the same trick: strip the edges, raise the case. Before counting anything over that column, it's worth checking whether it merged every duplicate.
tasks.goal: Understand whether string normalization is enough to make one outlet into one row.
tasks.predictQuestion: The export holds 104 different spellings of customer names, while the real number of outlets in it is 45. What does this code return?

options.label: 52: case and spaces collapsed, but seven outlets are written in two romanisations and stayed distinct
options.why: «Ichiba #1026» and «Itiba #1026» are one outlet, but a string method compares characters, and their first letters differ. It removes case and spaces; a differently spelled name it cannot.

options.label: 45: casting to one form gives exactly the real number of outlets
options.why: That would hold if every discrepancy came down to the form of the record. There's a third kind here (one name in two romanisations), and string normalization doesn't cure it.

options.label: 104: .str.upper() changes nothing, because customer names are already in one case
options.why: The case in this column really is uniform, but .str.strip() in the same chain removes the edge spaces, and that alone takes 104 spellings down to 52.

options.label: The code fails: .str.strip() and .str.upper() can't be chained
options.why: Both methods return a Series of strings, so the chain is valid; .str can be applied as many times in a row as you need.

hints: Look at what exactly differs between two spellings of one outlet: the case, the spaces, or the letters themselves.
A string method has no way of knowing that two dissimilar names mean the same thing.
tasks.explain: 52, not 45. Edge spaces and case are discrepancies of form: a string function removes them because it can see that the strings differ by nothing else. A different romanisation is a discrepancy of content: «Ichiba» and «Itiba» are made of different letters, and no amount of case folding brings them together. This is the boundary where string cleaning ends and entity matching begins: you need a mapping table, or a rule that folds the variants into one canonical form, that is, outside knowledge that these are one chain. The data itself doesn't carry that knowledge. The practical consequence is worse than it looks: after .str.strip().str.upper() the numbers look clean and are therefore more dangerous than the raw ones. A report over 52 customers will agree with itself, while seven outlets in it are counted twice, each with half of its turnover, and no duplicate check will show it.

tasks.title: One customer, two spellings
tasks.brief: customer_name in this same extract stores trailing/leading spaces on some rows: "Minori #1013 " and "Minori #1013"; these are two different values here, even though it's the same outlet.
tasks.goal: Count how many unique customer names will remain if leading/trailing spaces are removed.
hints: .str.strip() removes spaces only at the edges of a string, leaving spaces inside it untouched.
After normalizing, count with nunique(), as in the previous task.
tasks.explain: 104 unique values turn into 52, exactly half turned out to be the same customer with an extra space at the edge. .strip() is the most common first step when working with any raw extract: spaces aren't visible to the eye in a table, but they make two visually identical strings different for grouping and joining.

tasks.title: Weekly sales into monthly
tasks.brief: The «Aqualis» category manager wants monthly sales dynamics rather than weekly; weekly numbers swing too much to discuss in a meeting.
tasks.goal: From the weekly series weekly (already with a datetime index), return the monthly sum of units via resample('MS').
hints: resample('MS') re-buckets a time series onto month-start boundaries (Month Start), similar to GROUP BY month in SQL, but it requires the index to already be datetime.
resample needs an aggregating function afterward, .sum(), just like an ordinary groupby.
tasks.explain: resample only works on a datetime index; first the date is turned into an index (pd.to_datetime + set_index), and only then can resample('MS') find month boundaries. The idea is the same as GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', week_start) in SQL, but resample additionally understands the calendar and can work at any frequency (week, quarter, year) with no manual date formatting.

tasks.title: Why the first three weeks have no value
tasks.brief: An analyst smooths a weekly series with a 4-week rolling average and can't understand why the first three points of the chart have no value at all.
tasks.goal: Understand rolling()'s behavior at the start of a series.
tasks.predictQuestion: weekly is a series of weekly units, sorted by date, with no gaps at all. What will the first three values of rolling(4).mean() be?

options.label: NaN: a 4-week window has nothing to average yet, until 4 observations have accumulated
options.why: rolling(4) requires a full window by default: min_periods equals the window size unless set separately. For the first three weeks there's simply nothing to compute a 4-week average from.

options.label: 0: pandas substitutes zero until the window fills up
options.why: pandas never substitutes 0 for a missing value; that would distort the average. The correct signal for "not enough data yet" is NaN, not a number.

options.label: The average of whatever weeks are already available: first over one, then two, then three
options.why: That's how rolling(4, min_periods=1) would behave, but that isn't the default. Without an explicit min_periods, pandas waits for a full window of 4 values.

options.label: The series' first real value, repeated three times
options.why: rolling() doesn't fill the start of the series by repeating the first value; with an incomplete window it returns NaN by default, rather than trying to guess an average from missing weeks.

hints: rolling() has a min_periods parameter, and by default it equals the window size.
NaN at the start of a rolling series isn't an error, it's an honest signal that there's no full window here yet.
tasks.explain: min_periods = window size is the default behavior, and it's a deliberate library choice: an approximation from a partial window (an average of 1-2-3 observations instead of 4) would be a statistically different quantity, and pandas doesn't substitute it without an explicit request. If values are needed from the very start of the series, min_periods=1 changes that explicitly, not by default.

tasks.title: A smoothed series next to the source
tasks.brief: The same «Aqualis» weekly series is needed with 4-week smoothing next to the source data, so the chart doesn't show a weekly sawtooth.
tasks.goal: Add a rolling4 column to weekly with the rolling mean of units over the last 4 weeks.
hints: rolling(4) sets a 4-observation rolling-average window, the same number as ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW in SQL (sql-window-frame).
After .rolling(4) you need .mean(), just as after .groupby(...): rolling() on its own only defines the window, it doesn't compute a statistic.
tasks.explain: rolling(4).mean() is a direct equivalent of the window frame ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW from sql-window-frame: the window slides over the ordered series, including the current row and the three before it. The difference is in the notation: in SQL the frame is defined inside OVER(...), in pandas it's a separate call, .rolling(window_size), before the aggregating function.

tasks.title: The flag that landed nowhere
tasks.brief: An intern marks large sales with a flag directly on a filtered slice. The code runs without a single error, and a day later it turns out nothing changed.
tasks.goal: Understand what happens to the source table under two consecutive index lookups.
tasks.predictQuestion: The code runs without exceptions (pandas prints a warning but doesn't stop). Will a flag column appear in fact_sellout after this line?

options.label: No, flag won't appear anywhere: the column is added to a temporary object that is discarded immediately, and the source table doesn't change at all
options.why: fact_sellout[mask] creates a separate temporary object, a copy of the filtered rows with no connection to the original. ['flag'] = 1 modifies that copy specifically, and it ceases to exist the moment the line finishes executing.

options.label: Yes: flag will appear in fact_sellout for every row with revenue > 3000, and the rest will have NaN
options.why: That's what .loc[mask, 'flag'] = 1 would do, one lookup into the table instead of two. Here the second indexing, ['flag'], is applied not to fact_sellout but to a copy that has already separated from it.

options.label: Yes: flag will appear on every row of fact_sellout with the value 1, regardless of revenue
options.why: Even if the assignment did reach the original, the mask would confine it to rows with revenue > 3000. But it never reaches the original at all; the copy is discarded before anything can affect fact_sellout.

options.label: The code will fail with an error: you can't assign a column through two consecutive index lookups
options.why: There will be no error: pandas performs both operations and prints a warning (SettingWithCopyWarning), not an exception. That's exactly what makes the bug so treacherous; nothing signals explicitly that something went wrong.

hints: fact_sellout[mask] is already a separate object, not fact_sellout itself. The second [] works on that object, not on the source table.
The temporary object lives exactly until the end of the expression; you can't assign something to it and expect that to show up in the source table.
tasks.explain: pandas honestly warns about this (SettingWithCopyWarning), but doesn't halt execution, and if you don't pay attention to the warning, the bug looks like a complete absence of a bug: the code ran, and the data didn't change. The correct form is through .loc: fact_sellout.loc[fact_sellout['revenue'] > 3000, 'flag'] = 1, one lookup into the table instead of two.

tasks.title: Large sales as a separate table
tasks.brief: A logistics analyst wants a separate table of sales above the average revenue across all of fact_sellout, marked with is_large, without touching the source table and without relying on pandas warnings to notice it.
tasks.goal: Return the rows of fact_sellout where revenue is above the average for the whole table, with an extra column is_large=True, as a chain through .copy() and .assign(), with no intermediate assignment into a filtered slice.
hints: .copy() right after the filter says explicitly: from here on you're working with an independent table, not a view onto the source, and the warning stops appearing.
.assign(name=value) adds a column and returns a new table in that same call; the chain can continue without being broken by an intermediate variable.
tasks.explain: .copy() and .assign() are what turn the previous task from a trap into a working technique: .copy() explicitly fixes independence from the source table, instead of leaving pandas to guess whether this is a view or a copy, and .assign() adds a column while staying inside one chain of calls, rather than going through a separate df['col'] = .... It's precisely the absence of an extra intermediate variable and of direct assignment through [] that guards against the scenario that broke py-038.

tasks.title: The same flag, but done right
tasks.brief: The same "large sale" flag, but done right, through .loc, with no intermediate object that can be lost by accident.
tasks.goal: Set flag=1 directly in fact_sellout for rows with revenue > 3000, modifying the table in a single lookup through .loc.
hints: .loc[mask, 'column'] = value is one lookup into the table instead of two consecutive [][], so pandas knows exactly what you mean and no warning appears.
.copy() here is only so that fact_sellout isn't modified directly in this task; the .loc[...] = ... technique itself works without it, if modifying the table is what you actually intend.
tasks.explain: .loc[mask, 'column'] = value is a single operation instead of the two consecutive index lookups that left pandas unable to tell whether you were working with a view or a copy. The very same flag that failed to appear in py-038 lands reliably here, because there's no intermediate object that can be discarded by accident.

tasks.title: A region's priority without apply
tasks.brief: A colleague wrote the "region priority" column through apply(lambda row: ..., axis=1); on 16 regions that goes unnoticed, but the same technique on fact_sellout (118 thousand rows) will noticeably hang in the browser.
tasks.goal: Build a priority column for dim_region: 'key' for tier == 1, otherwise 'rest', through vectorized np.where and without apply().
hints: np.where(condition, if_true, if_false) is the vectorized replacement for apply(lambda row: ... if ... else ..., axis=1): the condition is checked for the whole column at once, not row after row.
np is already available in the task's code alongside pd and the tables; you can call it directly as np.where(...).
tasks.explain: apply(..., axis=1) calls a Python function separately for every row; on 16 regions that's 16 calls, and on fact_sellout it would be 118,449, each one carrying Python interpreter overhead on top of the check itself. np.where evaluates the condition once for the entire column in optimized NumPy code, the same result, but orders of magnitude faster on a large table, even though the difference isn't visible on a small one. Of the 16 regions, 4 come out as key and the other 12 as 'rest': the cheapest way to check that is value_counts() on the new column, a habit worth carrying from the very first step of exploration.

tasks.title: Same result, different price
tasks.brief: A colleague insists: "apply and a vectorized operation give the same result, so you can use either one, it's a matter of taste." On a small table the difference isn't visible; the question is what changes on a large one.
tasks.goal: Understand what exactly the difference is between apply(..., axis=1) and a vectorized operation, given that the result is identical.
tasks.predictQuestion: On dim_product's 47 rows both variants produce the same segment column. What happens if the same technique is applied to fact_sellout (118,449 rows)?

options.label: The result stays the same in both variants, but variant A will be noticeably slower: by orders of magnitude, not by percentages, because it calls a Python function separately on every row
options.why: apply(..., axis=1) is a Python row loop under the hood: on 118,449 rows that's 118,449 separate function calls, each with interpreter overhead. np.where performs the same comparison once for the whole column in vectorized NumPy code.

options.label: On a large table apply(..., axis=1) and np.where will give different results: apply is more accurate, because it sees the whole row
options.why: Both variants check the same condition (list_price > 300) and give an identical result regardless of the table's size. The fact that apply technically sees the whole row isn't used here and adds no accuracy.

options.label: np.where doesn't work on tables with more than a few thousand rows: you'd have to go back to apply
options.why: np.where has no size limit: NumPy's vectorized operations were built for large data arrays specifically; they don't degrade or give out as the number of rows grows.

options.label: There will be a speed difference, but a small one: within 10-20%, not critical for a task running in a browser
options.why: The difference is usually orders of magnitude (severalfold to tens of times over), not within 10-20%, which is exactly why apply(..., axis=1) on genuinely large tables can noticeably freeze the interface, while a vectorized operation doesn't.

hints: The result is identical; checking the values can't tell "bad" code from "good" here, the difference shows up only in speed.
apply(..., axis=1) is a row loop at the Python level; np.where is an operation at the NumPy level, with no Python loop at all.
tasks.explain: On small tables (like dim_product, 47 rows) the difference isn't visible to the eye; on fact_sellout it can be tens of times over, exactly what makes an analyst's code "hang" on a seemingly simple line. Since the values match, an ordinary check of the result won't catch the difference in approach: what needs practicing is recognizing the apply(lambda row: ..., axis=1) pattern as a candidate for replacement, not the result of running it.

tasks.title: A product label without row-by-row formatting
tasks.brief: The data schema builds a product label, "brand / category", through apply(lambda row: f'...', axis=1); it works, but it's recomputed from scratch on every change of filter, and on a large table that's felt.
tasks.goal: Build a label column = brand + ' / ' + category for dim_product in a vectorized way, without apply and without row-by-row string formatting.
hints: pandas string columns are added with the + operator just like ordinary Python strings, but element by element, for every row at once.
The separator ' / ' is an ordinary constant string between the two columns.
tasks.explain: Adding string columns with + is a vectorized operation: pandas concatenates values element by element for the whole column at once, with no function call on every row. apply(lambda row: f'{row["brand"]} / {row["category"]}', axis=1) produces the same text, but walks the rows in a Python loop, with the same overpayment on interpreter overhead as in py-041/py-042, just on a different operation: string formatting instead of comparing numbers.
